question: What part of the nervous system is mainly inflamed in meningitis?

options.A: Functional units of the cerebral cortex
options.B: Main motor tracts of the spinal cord
options.C: Vascular supply of the basal ganglia

explanation: Meningitis specifically targets the meninges, which are the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h1)

question: Why are central nervous system infections treated as critical emergencies?

options.A: Blood pressure drops to zero during the initial invasion
options.B: Rapid inflammation easily threatens life and brain function
options.C: Pathogens immediately destroy all peripheral nerve pathways
options.D: Surgical intervention is the only possible treatment method

explanation: The skull is a closed space, so rapid swelling can quickly compromise brain tissue and vital life functions. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h1)

question: How do germs typically move during retrograde axonal transport?

options.A: Via the lymphatic system into the thoracic duct first
options.B: Along peripheral nerves directly into the central nervous system
options.C: Through the bloodstream from a primary lung infection
options.D: Directly across the skull bone following a blunt trauma

explanation: Certain viruses use nerve fibers to travel upward toward the brain and spinal cord. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h2)

question: What happens directly when white blood cells flood the subarachnoid space?

options.A: Increased intracranial pressure and cerebral edema
options.B: Complete blockage of cerebrospinal fluid production
options.C: Permanent stabilization of systemic blood pressure
options.D: Immediate repair of all damaged nerve endings

explanation: The immune response causes inflammation and swelling inside the rigid skull, raising pressure on the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h2)

question: Which cerebrospinal fluid finding points most to bacterial meningitis?

options.B: Low glucose levels with high protein
options.D: Elevated glucose with zero white cells

explanation: Bacterial pathogens consume glucose rapidly and provoke a high protein response in the fluid. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h3)

question: A patient with fungal meningitis is most likely to have which underlying issue?
explanation: Fungal infections typically take advantage of weaknesses in immunocompromised hosts. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h3)

question: What is the main difference between meningitis and encephalitis?

options.A: Meningitis always includes localized pus collection
options.B: Encephalitis never causes any changes in mental status
options.C: Encephalitis involves direct inflammation of the brain tissue
options.D: Meningitis affects only the peripheral nervous system

explanation: Encephalitis affects the brain tissue itself, whereas meningitis affects the outer covering layers. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h4)

question: How does a brain abscess affect the inside of the skull?

options.A: It acts as a space-occupying lesion that raises pressure
options.B: It converts all surrounding bone into soft cartilage
options.C: It drains safely through the nasal passages on its own
options.D: It automatically dissolves without causing any swelling

explanation: A pus collection takes up extra volume inside the skull, leading to increased intracranial pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h4)

question: What physical finding shows a positive Brudzinski's sign?

options.A: Inability to straighten the leg when the patient's hip is flexed
options.B: Immediate dilation of both pupils when light is shone in one eye
options.C: Involuntary flexion of the hips and knees when the neck is flexed
options.D: Severe pain in the lower back during deep inspiration

explanation: Brudzinski's sign is positive when bending the neck forward triggers a reflexive bending of the legs at the hips and knees. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h5)

question: How does meningitis often present in an infant?

options.A: Sudden inability to track moving toys
options.B: A bulging fontanel and poor feeding
options.C: Exaggerated startle reflex to bright lights
options.D: Complaints of a sharp, throbbing leg cramp

explanation: Infants often show signs of increased intracranial pressure like a bulging soft spot and poor feeding instead of classic neck stiffness. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h5)

question: Between which vertebrae is a lumbar puncture needle usually inserted?
explanation: The puncture is safely performed in the lower back region below where the spinal cord ends. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h6)

question: Why is a CT scan sometimes done before a lumbar puncture?

options.A: To rule out a mass lesion that could cause brain herniation
options.B: To sterilize the skin surface where the needle will enter
options.C: To measure the exact volume of blood circulating in the brain
options.D: To replace the need for cerebrospinal fluid laboratory testing

explanation: Removing fluid when pressure is high and unequal can push the brain downward, leading to dangerous herniation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h6)

question: Which medication is often given alongside antibiotics to lower brain inflammation?
explanation: Corticosteroids like dexamethasone help reduce the damaging inflammation triggered by dying bacteria. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h7)

question: Why are antibiotics started immediately in severe cases before test results are ready?

options.A: Antibiotics improve the clarity of the cerebrospinal fluid sample
options.B: Laboratory tests are completely unreliable for bacterial detection
options.C: Pathogens will develop resistance if treatment waits for a culture
options.D: Delays in treatment drastically increase mortality and brain damage

explanation: Bacterial meningitis progresses so fast that waiting for lab results can be fatal or cause permanent harm. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h7)

question: How should the room be arranged for a patient with acute meningitis?

options.A: Keep the room quiet and dimly lit to reduce sensory irritation
options.B: Play loud music to keep the patient oriented to time
options.C: Encourage frequent visitors to maintain high social engagement
options.D: Provide bright fluorescent lighting to stimulate the visual cortex

explanation: Patients are often extremely sensitive to light and sound, so a calm and quiet environment is necessary. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h8)

question: Why is fluid intake carefully watched in patients with brain infections?

options.A: Patients will develop kidney failure if they drink any water
options.B: Dehydration helps shrink the bacterial count in the blood
options.C: Intravenous fluids replace the need for antibiotic therapy
options.D: Overhydration can worsen brain swelling and intracranial pressure

explanation: Too much fluid can increase swelling inside the rigid skull vault. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h8)

question: During which weather condition do meningitis outbreaks usually peak in the Nigerian meningitis belt?
explanation: Dry, dusty winds dry out the lining of the nose and throat, making it easier for bacteria to spread. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h9)

question: Why are preventive antibiotics given to people living closely with a meningitis patient?

options.A: To eradicate carriage and prevent transmission to others
options.B: To prevent the development of drug allergies later
options.C: To boost overall red blood cell production rapidly
options.D: To cure any chronic joint pain caused by the virus

explanation: Close contacts often carry the bacteria in their upper airway and need preventive medicine to stop new infections. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T17#GNS222_U3_T17_h9)
